To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

an empirical relationship exists between NHPs and humans in the pharmacokinetics of a subcutaneous macromolecule and this relationship can be used to support study design for a subsequent first-in-human investigation.

an empiric scaling factor of 0.75 was sufficient to predict the subcutaneous time course of a novel macromolecule for a first-in-man investigation, and that the scaling factor was consistent with the assumption of a constant absorption rate per unit surface area.

the absorption time course of a subcutaneous pegylated peptide in humans can be reasonably predicted from NHP data, and the prediction is improved by incorporating empiric scaling exponents based on body weight.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prediction of a macromolecule’s time course following subcutaneous (SC) administration in humans.
the development of an empirically based method for predicting the time course of subcutaneously administered peptide conjugates.
a macromolecule which has a high affinity for skin and which is absorbed from the subcutaneous space.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the scaling of the absorption of a pegylate peptide conjugate from NHPs to humans is feasible, but that a more precise prediction of human data would be obtained if the scaling factors were based on the human data.
the use of allometry in the prediction of the pharmacokinetics of subcutaneously administered pegylated peptide was not fully supported by this research.
a scaling factor of 0.75 for subcutaneous absorption of macromolecular drugs is a reasonable assumption, but it is not a perfect assumption.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of allometric scaling to predict the pharmacokinetic time course of a macromolecular peptide conjugate after subcutaneous delivery in humans was supported.
a first-in-human study of a pegylatic peptide conjugate could be designed with a reasonable expectation of success based on a scaling approach using NHP data.
the use of empiric scaling factors for the absorption process may be a useful approach for predicting the time course of macromolecules after subcutaneous delivery.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a first-in-human study of a subcutaneous administered peptide conjugate can be designed based on data from NHPs, provided that the pharmacokinetic time course of the compound is adequately characterized.
the scaling factors for clearance and volume can be obtained from the literature and that the absorption scaling factors may be empirically derived.
scaling of the subcutaneous absorption time course is possible, but that the exponents for scaling are not universal.
